This is Tanoura. 13th century to present.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tanoura originated from the Sufi whirling tradition, which was established by the mystic poet Rumi in the 13th century.
While the Mevlevi order in Turkey maintained the white-robed sema, the Egyptian form evolved into the tanoura, incorporating colorful skirts and becoming a distinct folk dance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tanoura is performed at Sufi festivals, moulids, and as a concert dance.
It serves as a visual representation of the cosmos and the connection between the divine and humanity, while also functioning as a form of entertainment.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dancer spins continuously, typically counter-clockwise, around the left foot.
The right foot provides the impetus for the rotation.
Arms are held with the right hand directed toward the sky and the left hand toward the earth.
Watch for Whirling.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is central to the performance, often featuring the ney (flute) and various percussion instruments.
The music is derived from the dhikr, a form of Islamic prayer and remembrance, and is intended to nourish the soul.
Listen for the ney, percussion.
The music is characterized by the haunting sound of the ney flute and steady, rhythmic percussion, creating a trance-like atmosphere suitable for long-duration spinning.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The primary costume is the tanoura, a heavy, multi-layered, and colorful skirt.
The colors represent different Sufi orders.
The dance is performed in various settings, including Sufi festivals, cultural heritage venues, and concert halls.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: While the performance version is secular, the dance originates from the sacred Sufi dhikr. Performers and observers should treat the spiritual origins with respect, particularly when performed in a religious context.
